node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample statistic versus population parameter
node.description: Distinguish a sample statistic from the population parameter it estimates in inference contexts.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling variability in senior inference
node.description: Explain why sample statistics vary from sample to sample and why that variation matters for inference.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling distribution centre
node.description: Identify the centre of a sampling distribution and connect it to the parameter being estimated under appropriate conditions.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling distribution spread
node.description: Interpret the spread of a sampling distribution as sampling error measured by standard error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Central limit theorem introduction
node.description: Use the central limit theorem to justify approximate normal sampling distributions for large samples in suitable contexts.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error for a sample proportion
node.description: Calculate or interpret the standard error of a sample proportion under binomial-style assumptions.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error for a sample mean
node.description: Calculate or interpret the standard error of a sample mean using population or sample standard deviation information as appropriate.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Confidence interval structure
node.description: Interpret a confidence interval as an estimate plus or minus a margin of error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Critical value for confidence level
node.description: Choose or interpret the critical value associated with a confidence level for common normal-based intervals.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Factors affecting margin of error
node.description: Explain how confidence level, variability and sample size affect the margin of error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Context interpretation of confidence intervals
node.description: Write a contextual interpretation of a confidence interval that refers to the population parameter and confidence method.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Conditions for proportion interval
node.description: Check randomisation, independence and success-failure conditions for a confidence interval for a proportion.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Conditions for mean interval
node.description: Check randomisation, independence and approximate-normal conditions for a confidence interval for a mean.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Hypothesis parameter statement
node.description: State null and alternative hypotheses using the relevant population parameter rather than sample statistics.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: One tailed and two tailed tests
node.description: Choose a one-tailed or two-tailed alternative hypothesis based on the research question.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Test statistic standardisation
node.description: Standardise the difference between an observed statistic and the null value using an appropriate standard error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: P-value as tail area
node.description: Interpret a p-value as a tail probability under the null model at least as extreme as the observed result.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare p-value with alpha
node.description: Make a hypothesis-test decision by comparing the p-value with the chosen significance level.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Contextual hypothesis test conclusion
node.description: Write a hypothesis-test conclusion in context using evidence language rather than proof language.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Type I error in context
node.description: Describe a Type I error in the original context as rejecting a true null hypothesis.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Type II error in context
node.description: Describe a Type II error in the original context as failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Statistic estimates parameter
node.description: A sample statistic is used to estimate an unknown population parameter.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Larger sample reduces standard error
node.description: For common estimators, increasing sample size reduces standard error when other factors are unchanged.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interval is estimate plus margin
node.description: A common confidence interval is formed from an estimate plus and minus a margin of error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Hypotheses use parameters
node.description: Formal hypotheses should be stated about population parameters, not observed sample statistics.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Type I rejects true null
node.description: A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Statistic equals parameter
node.description: Learner treats a sample statistic as exactly equal to the population parameter rather than as an estimate subject to sampling variability.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Higher confidence gives narrower interval
node.description: Learner thinks increasing the confidence level makes a confidence interval narrower when other factors are unchanged.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Hypothesis about sample statistic
node.description: Learner states null and alternative hypotheses about the observed sample statistic rather than the population parameter.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: P-value as effect size
node.description: Learner interprets a smaller p-value as measuring the size or practical importance of an effect.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fail to reject proves null
node.description: Learner treats failing to reject the null hypothesis as proof that the null hypothesis is true.

edge.rationale: Distinguishing statistics and parameters is central to statistical inference.
The centre of a sampling distribution is a core sampling-distribution feature.
Standard error measures the spread of a sampling distribution.
Understanding confidence intervals includes recognising estimate-plus-margin structure.
Correct hypothesis statements are a core part of null and alternative hypotheses.
Tail-area interpretation is central to p-value meaning.
Senior inference builds on earlier sample-to-population reasoning.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot distinguish a sample result from a population claim.

edge.rationale: Sampling variability is understood relative to the statistic used to estimate a parameter.
edge.failure_signal: Learner expects repeated random samples to give exactly the same statistic.

edge.rationale: A sampling distribution's centre is interpreted after understanding sample-to-sample variation.
edge.failure_signal: Learner confuses the centre of the sampling distribution with one observed sample statistic.

edge.rationale: Describing spread builds on knowing what distribution and centre are being described.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats standard error as the same as raw-data standard deviation.

edge.rationale: The central limit theorem describes conditions under which sampling distributions are approximately normal.
edge.failure_signal: Learner applies normal approximation without considering sample size or shape conditions.

edge.rationale: The proportion formula is a specific standard-error case.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses raw proportion as standard error or omits sample size.

edge.rationale: The mean formula is a specific standard-error case.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses standard deviation as standard error without dividing by square root of sample size.

edge.rationale: Confidence intervals use standard error as part of their margin of error.
edge.failure_signal: Learner gives only the point estimate without uncertainty width.

edge.rationale: Critical values scale the standard error in the interval structure.
edge.failure_signal: Learner chooses a critical value unrelated to the confidence level or tail area.

edge.rationale: Margin of error depends on critical value, variability and sample size.
edge.failure_signal: Learner predicts margin changes in the wrong direction when confidence or sample size changes.

edge.rationale: Contextual interpretation requires understanding confidence interval meaning.
edge.failure_signal: Learner says the probability the fixed interval contains the parameter is the confidence level.

edge.rationale: Proportion interval conditions are a specific application of inference assumptions and conditions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner calculates an interval without checking randomisation, independence or success-failure counts.

edge.rationale: Mean interval conditions are a specific application of inference assumptions and conditions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses a mean interval when data shape or sample size conditions are not reasonable.

edge.rationale: Formal hypotheses must refer to population parameters rather than observed sample statistics.
edge.failure_signal: Learner writes hypotheses using the sample statistic value.

edge.rationale: Tail direction is chosen from the alternative hypothesis and research question.
edge.failure_signal: Learner chooses two-tailed by default or mismatches the directional claim.

edge.rationale: A test statistic standardises the observed difference by an appropriate standard error.
edge.failure_signal: Learner calculates raw difference but cannot put it on a reference distribution scale.

edge.rationale: P-value tail area is interpreted from the test statistic under the null distribution.
edge.failure_signal: Learner interprets p-value as probability the null hypothesis is true.

edge.rationale: Hypothesis-test decisions require interpreting the p-value before comparing it to alpha.
edge.failure_signal: Learner reverses the reject/fail-to-reject decision rule.

edge.rationale: A contextual conclusion follows after making the p-value versus alpha decision.
edge.failure_signal: Learner states a decision without connecting it back to the original context.

edge.rationale: Contextual Type I error statements build on the formal Type I and Type II distinction.
edge.failure_signal: Learner swaps Type I and Type II errors in context.

edge.rationale: Type II contextual interpretation is paired with Type I interpretation and requires distinguishing the two outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner defines both errors as rejecting the null.
